0.value:
Makes an exponential (Poisson) window: exp(-|n - centre| / tau), a peak with straight-sided fall-offs on a log scale.

Use it to taper a frame of samples before a Fourier transform (t.rfft), or as a smoothing kernel or fade shape: it is a list of m weights, at most 1, that rise towards the middle.

THE SHAPE:
A point at the centre, falling away exponentially on both sides: tau is how many samples it takes to fall to about a third. Unlike the cosine windows it never reaches zero and has a sharp peak rather than a rounded top. Use it where recent samples should count more than distant ones, or for damped (decaying) signals.

SYNTAX:
t.window.exponential
No arguments: set the length and the rest on the node.

EXAMPLE:
t.window.exponential

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

(button, the first inlet):
Makes the window and sends it. Anything arriving here triggers it; in the demo a metro bangs it ten times a second so the plot follows your edits. Nothing else on the node sends by itself.

type (menu):
Which window. Choosing another one turns this node into that window - the title changes and the parameter boxes change to suit - so one node can audition them all.

m (int):
The length: how many values. Default 256, smallest 1. Match it to the number of samples in the frame you are going to multiply.

center (float, also an inlet):
Where the peak sits, in samples. Used ONLY when sym is off: with sym on the peak is always in the middle and this box is ignored. Default 1.0, which with sym off puts the peak at the second sample.

tau (float, also an inlet):
How fast the sides fall, in samples. Default 1.0, which for m 256 is a spike only a couple of samples wide; 40 or so gives a visible shape. Must be greater than 0; anything else prints an error and sends nothing.

sym (checkbox, default on):
On: SYMMETRIC - the window rises and falls the same way and both ends are the edge value. Right for designing filters. Off: PERIODIC - computed as if one sample longer and the last sample dropped, so a row of them laid end to end repeats exactly. That is the version to use before an FFT.

device / dtype / requires_grad:
Where the tensor is made (cpu by default), its number type (float32 by default) and whether gradients flow through it.

OUTPUTS:

window tensor out:
A 1-D tensor of m values, at most 1. Multiply a frame by it (a * node does tensors) before t.rfft.

WHAT A WINDOW IS FOR:
Cutting a frame out of a longer signal leaves ragged ends: unless the frame happens to hold a whole number of cycles, the last sample does not meet the first, and t.rfft reads that jump as extra frequencies smeared around every real one (LEAKAGE - drag the slider on the t.rfft page to 10.5 cycles to see it). Multiplying by a window fades the frame in and out so the ends meet at or near zero. The price is that each spectral spike gets wider. Every window is a different bargain between a narrow spike (the main lobe) and quiet surroundings (the side lobes).

READING THE DEMO:
The plot draws the window, first value on the left; the strip under it is the same values as shades (dark 0, bright 1). Drag the slider and the shape follows.

RELATED:
t.window.gaussian, t.window.kaiser and t.window.hann are on their own pages. t.rfft is what a window usually feeds; the type menu on this node switches to any other window.
